# Association of Anti-Ro52 Seropositive Interstitial Lung Disease With a Higher Risk of Disease Progression and Mortality

**Authors:** Ryosuke Imai; Rene S. Bermea; Sophia H. Zhao; Sydney B. Montesi; Anjali Singh; Bess M. Flashner; Andrew J. Synn; Julia K. Munchel; Mary B. Rice; Alyssa Soskis; Barry S. Shea; Robert W. Hallowell

## Abstract

Identifying biomarkers is vital for interstitial lung disease (ILD) management and prognostication. Although anti-Ro52 antibodies frequently are detected in autoimmune diseases, their significance in ILD remains unclear.

What is the prognostic significance of anti-Ro52 antibody positivity in patients with ILD?

This retrospective cohort study used an ILD registry of patients seen at an academic tertiary hospital’s ILD clinic between 2015 and 2024. All patients with a diagnosis of ILD and tested for anti-Ro52 antibody status were divided into anti-Ro52 positive and negative groups. The primary outcome was ILD progression or all-cause death. ILD progression was defined as any of the following: hospitalization because of ILD, absolute decline in FVC of ≥ 10% predicted from baseline, or lung transplantation. The Kaplan-Meier method and Cox proportional hazards regression model were used for survival analysis.

Of 1,026 patients tested for the anti-Ro52 antibody (median age, 70 years; 52% male), 154 patients (15%) showed positive anti-Ro52 results. Underlying ILD subtypes were as follows: interstitial pneumonia with autoimmune features (n = 489 [48%]), connective tissue disease-associated ILD (n = 132 [13%]), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (n = 103 [10%]), hypersensitivity pneumonitis (n = 61 [6%]), and other idiopathic ILD (n = 241 [24%]). The anti-Ro52-positive group was younger (median age, 67 years vs 70 years), was more likely to have connective tissue disease (28% vs 10%), and more frequently showed copositive results for myositis-specific antibody (29% vs 16%). After a median follow-up of 25.6 months, patients with positive anti-Ro52 findings showed a higher risk of ILD progression or death (hazard ratio, 2.10; 95% CI, 1.61-2.73; P < .001) and showed a higher risk of lung transplantation or death (hazard ratio, 1.61; 95% CI, 1.11-2.35; P = .014) on multivariable analysis.

Our results indicate that Anti-Ro52-seropositive ILD is associated with significantly worse progression-free and transplant-free survival and may inform disease prognostication and monitoring.

## Abstract

Take-Home PointsStudy Question: Does anti-Ro52 seropositivity impact interstitial lung disease (ILD) prognosis?Results: Our results indicate that anti-Ro52 seropositivity is associated with worse progression-free and transplant-free survival in patients with ILD.Interpretation: Anti-Ro52 may be an independent risk factor for poor prognosis, highlighting the need for close monitoring for disease progression.

Interstitial lung disease (ILD) encompasses a group of disorders characterized by varying degrees of inflammation and pulmonary fibrosis, arising from a range of causes.1,2 Although specific ILD subtypes are well recognized, a subset of patients with ILD experience disease progression that leads to worsening lung function, symptoms, and quality of life.3 With the advent of antifibrotic therapies, now approved not only for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) but also for progressive fibrotic ILD,4,5 identifying predictors of disease progression has become increasingly important for optimizing patient management.

Interest in defining the prognostic significance of the anti-Ro52 antibody, which targets the Ro52/TRIM21 protein, is growing.6 Several studies have reported an association between anti-Ro52 positivity and worse clinical outcomes in patients with various connective tissue diseases (CTDs), such as polymyositis, dermatomyositis, systemic lupus erythematosus, Sjögren syndrome, mixed CTD, and systemic sclerosis.7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 However, this association primarily has been studied in patients with established CTDs, and not all individuals in those studies had ILD. Furthermore, the impact of its presence in patients who do not meet clinical criteria for CTD—such as those with interstitial pneumonia with autoimmune features (IPAF)2 or other idiopathic ILDs—remains unclear. Our group previously reported that patients with ILD with an anti-Ro52 antibody exhibit clinical features and outcomes similar to those with anti-Ro52 antibodies and the presence of a myositis-specific antibody.13

Building on these findings, we aimed to investigate how the existence of anti-Ro52 antibodies affects the prognosis of ILD. To address this clinical question, a retrospective cohort study was conducted. We hypothesized that patients with ILD with anti-Ro52 antibodies would have a poorer prognosis compared with those without anti-Ro52 antibodies. Below, we present what we believe to be the largest study to date on the prognostic impact of anti-Ro52 antibodies in ILD.

## Study Design and Methods

### Study Design and Patients

This retrospective cohort study, approved by the Mass General Brigham institutional review board (Identifier: 2022P001829), was conducted at Massachusetts General Hospital, an academic tertiary hospital in the United States. Patients with ILD from our institutional ILD registry who were tested for the anti-Ro52 antibody at diagnosis were included. The registry comprises 2 combined cohorts. The first is a laboratory-identified cohort, which includes all patients with ILD identified through a query of the clinical laboratory database who underwent MyoMarker 3 or MyoMarker 3 Plus Profile testing (RDL Reference Laboratory) or EUROLINE Autoimmune Inflammatory Myopathies 16 Ag immunoassay (Euroimmun) between June 2020 and May 2024. These tests were ordered within our institution in both outpatient and inpatient settings. Although the precise clinical indications and ordering specialties were not always recorded, all patients in this cohort were confirmed to have ILD and subsequently were evaluated in the ILD clinic. The second is a clinician-referred cohort, which comprises patients with ILD who were evaluated by and received a diagnosis from pulmonologists in the ILD clinic and were entered into the ILD registry between January 2015 and May 2024, without initial inclusion through the laboratory-based method. Although the laboratory-identified cohort aims to capture all patients in the ILD clinic tested for anti-Ro52 antibodies, it may miss individuals who did not use our institution’s laboratory for testing. Therefore, to ensure comprehensive representation of patients from the ILD clinic, the clinician-referred cohort also was included, allowing systematic identification of individuals who underwent anti-Ro52 antibody testing and enhancing the overall completeness of the ILD registry. Previous work published by members of our group in 2019 includes a small subset of patients limited to the clinician-referred cohort.13 Patients with ILD caused by drugs, radiation, or infection, as well as those without follow-up or missing baseline FVC values, were excluded. ### Data Collection

Medical records were reviewed retrospectively to gather demographic information, comorbidities, autoantibody data, and radiologic data at the time the patients were evaluated initially in the ILD clinic. CT scan patterns were classified into usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP), nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, organizing pneumonia, nonspecific interstitial pneumonia with organizing pneumonia overlap, lymphoid interstitial pneumonia, or unclassifiable or other, based on a previous study15 and the official radiology report by board-certified radiologists specializing in thoracic imaging. UIP was defined as either definite or probable UIP, and the hypersensitivity pneumonitis pattern was classified as other. If the radiologist’s report did not mention specific patterns, the case was considered to be unclassifiable. Additionally, we collected pulmonary function test data, including FVC and diffusing capacity of the lungs for carbon monoxide (Dlco), which were measured routinely at baseline and every follow-up visit. ILD-targeted therapy, including immunosuppressants and antifibrotic agents, was treated as a time-varying variable, with patients considered exposed from the time of treatment initiation onward. Clinical outcomes, including ILD-related hospitalizations, lung transplantation, and death, also were recorded. To determine the ILD subtype, a board-certified pulmonologist (R. I., R. S. B., or R. W. H.) reviewed the medical records and determined the final ILD subtype among CTD-associated ILD (CTD-ILD), IPAF, IPF, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, or other idiopathic ILD according to the current guidelines.16,17 CTD was defined based on diagnosis by the patient’s treating rheumatologist, and IPAF was adjudicated according to published criteria2 through chart review.

### Autoantibody Measurement

At our institutional ILD outpatient clinic, patients routinely undergo screening for CTD-related antibodies as part of a diagnostic evaluation for ILD. However, anti-Ro52 antibody testing is not performed as a routine test; instead, it is ordered at the discretion of the attending physician based on clinical assessments. Anti-Ro52 antibody testing was carried out either with the MyoMarker 3 Profile, the MyoMarker 3 Plus Profile, the EUROLINE Autoimmune Inflammatory Myopathies 16 Ag immunoassay, or the Extended Myositis Panel (ARUP Laboratories). The results of other autoantibodies collected as part of the ILD serologic workup also were recorded: antinuclear antibody; rheumatoid factor; cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody; double-stranded DNA antibody; Ro60 antibody; SSB antibody; ribonucleoprotein antibody; Smith antibody; scleroderma-70 antibody; Ku antibody; polymyositis-scleroderma antibody; antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody; and myositis-specific antibodies, including Jo-1, PL-7, PL-12, EJ, OJ, Mi-2 antibody, melanoma differentiation-associated protein 5 antibody, signal recognition particle antibody, nuclear matrix protein 2 antibody, and transcriptional intermediary factor 1-γ antibody. Positivity for antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor was determined based on the IPAF criteria,2 whereas positivity for the other autoantibodies was defined as exceeding the respective normal range established for each test.

### Outcome Measures

Our primary outcomes included ILD progression or all-cause death. ILD progression was defined as a composite of the following: (1) nonelective hospitalization because of ILD, (2) absolute decline in FVC value of ≥ 10% predicted from baseline, and (3) lung transplantation. Hospitalization because of ILD was defined as admissions with respiratory failure primarily attributable to an ILD exacerbation. We recognized the inherent difficulty in distinguishing ILD exacerbation from other potential causes of hospitalization, such as infections. To address this, we conducted a thorough chart review for each patient, assessing clinical records, radiographic findings, laboratory results, and any microbiologic data to exclude hospitalizations primarily resulting from infections or other non-ILD exacerbation causes. Patients for whom respiratory failure was deemed to result from infections or other causes were excluded. ILD progression-free survival was assessed as time from the first visit with ILD diagnosis either to ILD progression or death or to the end of study follow-up (August 16, 2024), whichever happened first. Secondary outcomes included transplant-free survival, defined as the time from the first ILD diagnosis visit to lung transplantation or death, and the annual rate of change in FVC and Dlco.

### Statistical Analysis

The included patients were assigned to anti-Ro52-positive and anti-Ro52-negative groups. Continuous variables were presented as mean (SD) or median (interquartile range) and were compared using the Student t test or Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical variables were reported as No. (%) and were compared using the χ2 test or Fisher exact test, as appropriate.

ILD progression-free survival and transplant-free survival were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier curves and were compared using the log-rank test. Hazard ratios (HRs) for primary outcomes were estimated using Cox proportional hazards regression models adjusted for age, sex, smoking history, COPD, ILD subtype, baseline FVC and Dlco, and UIP pattern as time-fixed covariates, with immunosuppressant and antifibrotic use as time-varying covariates. We performed 2 subgroup analyses. The first was stratified by ILD subtype, CTD-ILD and IPAF, to address potential confounding related to ILD subtype, with IPF included as the reference group for comparison. The second analysis focused on patients with CTD-ILD or IPAF and was stratified by myositis-specific antibody positivity to account for potential confounding resulting from the presence of autoantibodies. We used Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox models to evaluate the association between anti-Ro52 antibody findings and outcomes within each subgroup. The proportional-hazard assumption was assessed by scaled Schoenfeld residuals. Among the covariates, missing data were observed in Dlco (86 patients [8.38%]) and smoking history (16 patients [1.56%]). To address this, multiple imputation via chained equations was performed under the assumption of missingness at random. Predictive mean matching was applied, generating 50 imputations to enhance the stability of parameter estimates.

To analyze the annual rate of change in pulmonary function test results, we used mixed-effects models incorporating fixed covariates: anti-Ro52 antibody status, time from baseline, age, sex, smoking history, ILD subtype, baseline FVC, UIP pattern, and the use of immunosuppressants or antifibrotic agents, along with random intercepts and slopes for individuals. We included status × time interactions to assess differences in the annual rate of absolute FVC and Dlco values between the anti-Ro52-positive and anti-Ro52-negative groups. We also conducted subgroup analyses by ILD subtype to evaluate the annual rate of change in pulmonary function test results within each subgroup. The linearity assumption of the mixed-effects models was assessed by plotting the model residuals against time and by adding polynomial terms for time. The final model was chosen using Akaike information criterion. Only complete cases were included in this analysis.

An additional analysis was conducted to examine the association between anti-Ro52 antibody titers and the risk of ILD progression or mortality in a laboratory-referred cohort of patients with positive results for anti-Ro52 antibodies using the MyoMarker 3 or MyoMarker 3 Plus Profile. This assay uses enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and radioimmunoprecipitation assay gel radiography, with antibody titers classified as weak positive (20-39 units), moderate positive (40-80 units), and strong positive (> 80 units).18 Kaplan-Meier analysis was performed to compare ILD progression-free survival across these categories. Cox proportional hazards regression models were used to estimate the HRs for ILD progression or death, with titers analyzed as a log-transformed continuous variable (model 1) and a categorical variable (model 2).

Because this was a retrospective cohort study, no formal sample size calculation was performed. The study population was determined based on all eligible patients who met the inclusion criteria within the study period. Data were analyzed using R version 3.5.2 software (R Foundation for Statistical Computing). Hypothesis tests were 2-tailed and used a 5% significance level.

## Results

Among 1,250 patients with ILD (1,081 from the laboratory-identified cohort and 169 from the clinician-referred cohort), 1,202 patients underwent testing for anti-Ro52 antibody. After applying the exclusion criteria, 1,026 patients were included: 154 patients (15%) showed positive anti-Ro52 results and 872 patients (85%) showed negative anti-Ro52 results (Fig 1). The median age was 70 years (interquartile range, 63-76 years), and 52% of patients were male. The distribution of ILD subtypes was as follows: IPAF, n = 489 (47.7%); CTD-ILD, n = 132 (12.9%); IPF, n = 103 (10.0%); hypersensitivity pneumonitis, n = 61 (5.9%); and other idiopathic ILD, n = 241 (23.5%) (Table 1). The anti-Ro52-positive group was younger, more likely to have CTD and IPAF, and less likely to have coronary artery disease and to demonstrate a radiologic UIP pattern. Patients with positive anti-Ro52 findings also had higher rate of concurrent positive results for anti-Ro60, anti-SSB, and myositis-specific antibodies (Table 1). After a median follow-up of 26.8 months and 25.4 months for the anti-Ro52-positive and anti-Ro52-negative groups, respectively, the anti-Ro52-positive group more often received immunosuppressants, whereas the anti-Ro52-negative group more frequently was prescribed antifibrotics (Table 2). Among patients excluding those with CTD-ILD, the anti-Ro52-positive group remained less likely to exhibit a UIP pattern, had higher anti-Ro60 and myositis-specific antibody rates, and was more likely to receive immunosuppressants, with no differences in age or comorbidities between groups (e-Table 2, Table 3). Figure 2 shows the Kaplan-Meier curves for ILD progression-free survival (Fig 2A) and transplant-free survival (Fig 2B) stratified by the presence of anti-Ro52 antibodies. At 3 years, the estimated cumulative incidence of ILD progression or death was 53.4% (95% CI, 42.6%-62.2%) in the anti-Ro52-positive group compared with 32.9% (95% CI, 28.7%-36.9%) in the anti-Ro52-negative group. For lung transplant or death, the estimated cumulative incidence at 3 years was 19.7% (95% CI, 11.7%-27.0%) in the anti-Ro52-positive group compared with 13.8% (95% CI, 10.7%-16.7%) in the anti-Ro52-negative group. Multivariable analysis using a Cox proportional hazards regression model showed that anti-Ro52 positivity was associated with a higher risk of ILD progression or death (HR, 2.10; 95% CI, 1.61-2.73; P < .001) and lung transplant or death (HR, 1.61; 95% CI, 1.11-2.35; P = .014) (Table 3). The proportional hazards assumption was verified using Schoenfeld residuals (e-Fig 1). ## Discussion

To our knowledge, this is the largest study to date on the prognostic impact of anti-Ro52 antibodies in ILD and highlights the importance of measuring anti-Ro52 for predicting progressive ILD phenotypes. We demonstrated that among patients with ILD, the presence of anti-Ro52 antibodies was associated with higher rates of ILD progression and significantly worse progression-free and transplant-free survival. In subgroup analyses of patients with CTD-ILD and IPAF, the anti-Ro52-positive group consistently showed worse ILD progression-free survival than the anti-Ro52-negative group. Furthermore, this trend persisted regardless of myositis-specific antibody status, within the population with CTD-ILD or IPAF.

This study found a clear association between positive anti-Ro52 antibody findings and poor prognosis across the overall cohort. However, the anti-Ro52-positive group consisted predominantly of patients with CTD-ILD or IPAF, which could introduce potential bias because of the skewed distribution of ILD subtypes. To address this limitation, we performed subgroup analyses for CTD-ILD and IPAF, yielding consistent results across both subgroups. Although the association between anti-Ro52 positivity and poor prognosis aligns with previous smaller retrospective studies focused on patients with CTD-ILD,7, 8, 9,19,20 our work further highlights the prognostic impact of anti-Ro52 positivity in patients who do not meet the diagnostic criteria for CTD. Additionally, given the severe prognosis associated with anti-MDA5-positive ILD,11 which is one of the myositis-specific antibodies, it is crucial to consider potential confounding when interpreting the relationship between anti-Ro52 and ILD prognosis. However, our subgroup analysis demonstrated that anti-Ro52 is an independent predictor of poor prognosis in ILD, regardless of myositis-specific antibody positivity, suggesting its critical role in disease progression. Our study expands on our group’s previously published findings from a much smaller subset of patients in this cohort with positive anti-Ro52 results,13 which found that patients with anti-Ro52 antibodies had similar outcomes, regardless of whether copositive myositis-specific antibody findings were present. Our current study not only confirmed these findings with a much larger sample size and additional data points, but also compared outcomes between patients with anti-Ro52 positive and negative findings. However, we do acknowledge that some subgroups had limited sample sizes, leading to wide CIs, and no clear association was observed between anti-Ro52 positivity results and transplantation or death in the subgroups with CTD-ILD and myositis-specific antibody-negative CTD-ILD or IPAF.

Our findings are supported by biological plausibility. Previous studies showed that Ro52/TRIM21 overexpression can increase autoantibody production and can induce type I interferons along with proinflammatory cytokines, such as IL-6, IL-12, IL-23, and tumor necrosis factor-α.6 Type I interferons stimulate CX3CL secretion, which recruits CX3CR1+ M2 macrophages to the lungs, where they release transforming growth factor β to promote pulmonary fibrosis.21 These cytokines are linked closely to fibrosis pathways and a poor prognosis in ILD.21, 22, 23 Thus, these findings provide further clinical support that anti-Ro52 positivity is associated with worse ILD outcomes.

Interestingly, when examining the individual components of the composite outcome of ILD progression, hospitalization because of ILD seemed to be the primary driver of the observed differences. We found no significant difference between the anti-Ro52-positive and anti-Ro52-negative groups in the proportion of patients with a ≥ 10% decline in FVC or in the annual change in FVC. This might suggest that acute exacerbations of ILD are more frequent in the anti-Ro52-positive group and may explain in part the association between anti-Ro52 positivity and rapidly progressive ILD, as reported in previous studies.24, 25, 26 The reason for the lack of significant difference in the overall decline in pulmonary function test results between the 2 groups remains unclear. Possible explanations include differences in treatment responses, unadjusted baseline disease severity in the model, or the episodic nature of exacerbations in the anti-Ro52-positive group. Further research is needed to understand better the long-term patterns of lung function and treatment responses in this subset of patients with ILD, as well as the factors contributing to the higher mortality observed in these patients.

A key limitation of our study is the variability in the timing and conditions of anti-Ro52 antibody measurement. Autoantibody levels may have been affected by the time since disease onset or the use of immunosuppressants, likely leading to underestimation of prevalence. Additionally, different anti-Ro52 assays could have varying sensitivities and specificities, which may impact the accuracy of our findings further. However, in real-world practice, many patients with ILD undergo autoantibody testing after some time has passed or while receiving immunosuppressants, making our findings relevant to clinical settings. Another limitation is that the decision to test for anti-Ro52 antibodies was made by the attending physicians, meaning that the cohort tested for anti-Ro52 may not be representative of all patients with ILD. This selection bias likely contributed to the higher proportion of patients with CTD or IPAF diagnoses who demonstrated anti-Ro52-positive findings and the lower representation of patients with IPF in our study. This selection bias reduces the external validity of our findings to broader ILD populations. Additionally, not all ILD subtypes were determined through formal multidisciplinary discussions; rather, some final diagnoses were confirmed retrospectively by pulmonologists using clinical and radiologic data, supplemented by rheumatologist notes. This approach could lead to misclassification, especially if certain patients with possible CTD-ILD were never referred to, or formally assessed by, rheumatologists. Such misclassification may have attenuated or amplified observed differences between groups. Despite these limitations, our methodology closely mirrors typical clinical workflows, enhancing the practical relevance of our results. However, the generalizability of these findings may be limited to settings with similar referral patterns and testing practices. Future investigations using standardized multidisciplinary discussion protocols, uniform test methods, and clearly defined treatment timelines will be essential to validate and extend these observations.

## Interpretation

In this retrospective cohort of patients with ILD, anti-Ro52 seropositivity was associated significantly with higher rates of ILD progression and reduced progression-free and transplant-free survival. Importantly, anti-Ro52 positivity served as an independent risk factor for disease progression, regardless of CTD diagnosis or co-occurrence with myositis-specific antibodies. Therefore, patients with ILD and anti-Ro52 autoantibodies require close monitoring for disease progression.

# Abstract

Introduction: Few studies have thoroughly investigated the factors influencing the clinical course of pneumothorax at each stage of treatment. This study aimed to address this gap by examining these factors.

Methods: We conducted a single-center retrospective study involving patients with pneumothorax aged 20 years or older admitted to our hospital. Patients were divided into two groups: those successfully treated with chest tube drainage alone (Group A) and those who required additional treatment (Group B). Excluding patients requiring surgical treatment, patients in Group B were subsequently divided into two groups: those successfully treated with non-surgical secondary treatments (Group C) and those who were not (Group D). Clinical factors were compared between Groups A and B and between Groups C and D.

Results: Three hundred and ninety-five patients were included in this analysis. A comparison between Group A (148 patients) and B (247 patients) revealed significant differences in the presence of interstitial lung disease (ILD) (6.1% vs. 13.8%, p < 0.05) and pneumothorax history (20.4% vs. 42.5%, p < 0.05). Among patients in Group B, 172 underwent surgery as the next treatment, while 75 received non-surgical treatment after chest tube drainage. Significant differences were observed between Group C (27 patients) and D (48 patients) in heavy smoking history (33.3% vs. 62.5%, p < 0.05) and presence of ILD (25.9% vs. 52.1%, p < 0.05).

Conclusion: Patients with a history of ILD are more likely to require additional treatment after chest tube drainage.

## Introduction

In cases of clinically significant pneumothorax requiring intervention, a chest tube is placed for drainage. If the air leak persists, additional interventions are considered; when surgery is not feasible, alternative treatments such as pleurodesis, endobronchial valves, or endobronchial Watanabe spigot (EWS) may be employed [1,2]. Patients with poor cardiopulmonary reserve, including those with interstitial lung disease (ILD) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), often present with inoperable cases, making secondary pneumothorax in these conditions particularly challenging to manage [3-5]. However, few studies have examined the factors influencing treatment at various stages, including during chest tube placement or non-operative approaches in inoperable cases. Therefore, this study aimed to identify patients unlikely to be successfully treated with chest tube drainage alone and to determine the factors contributing to the failure of non-surgical treatment in inoperable cases. Additionally, the success rate of each nonoperative treatment was evaluated.

## Materials And Methods

## Patients

We conducted a single-center, retrospective study of patients aged 20 years or older who were admitted to our hospital with pneumothorax between January 1, 2011, and March 31, 2022. Patients with traumatic or medically induced pneumothorax, those without chest tube drainage, those transferred to other hospitals, and those who died on the day of admission were excluded from the study. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee of St. Luke’s International Hospital (approval number: 22-J013, approval date: August 18, 2022). Procedures followed were in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

Patients were divided into two groups: those with a pneumothorax that resolved with chest tube drainage alone (Group A) and those with a pneumothorax that did not resolve with chest tube drainage alone (Group B). After excluding patients who underwent surgery as a secondary treatment from Group B, the remaining patients were further classified into those with a pneumothorax that resolved with non-surgical secondary

Clinical factors were compared between Groups A and B and between Groups C and D. Variables assessed included age, sex, history of heavy smoking (30 pack-years or more), serum albumin level, comorbidities (COPD, ILD, or history of pneumothorax), treatment type, and length of hospital stay, all of which were obtained from previous medical records. “Resolution” was defined as “the absence of air accumulation in the pleural cavity on chest radiography within 24 hours of chest tube removal,” whereas “no resolution” was defined as a prolonged air leak lasting more than 48 hours. Heavy smoking history was defined as 30 packyears or more, in accordance with the definition of the Lung Cancer Screening Guidelines 2022 of the Japanese Lung Cancer Society [6]. Data on COPD and ILD were extracted from the patient’s medical histories. The non-surgical success rate was calculated as the proportion of resolutions achieved relative to the total number of treatments administered at each stage (first, second, third, fourth, etc.). For example, if a single patient was treated with autologous blood, EWS, and OK-432, each was counted as a separate treatment. The analysis included two groups of patients: all patients who received non-surgical secondary treatment and those with a pneumothorax that did not resolve with non-surgical secondary treatments.

## Pneumothorax treatment practice

The indication for surgery was determined by the surgeon upon admission. Generally, non-surgical treatments, typically autologous blood or OK-432 for pleurodesis, were initially performed, with the final treatment decision determined by the treating physician. Owing to insurance restrictions, talc was not used until March 2022. In cases of incomplete lung expansion, the attending physician decided whether to add or replace the tube or perform EWS.

## Statistical analysis

Categorical variables were compared using Fisher’s exact test, while continuous variables were compared using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (equivalent to the Mann-Whitney U test; we report the W statistic). To identify risk factors for treatment failure, a multivariable logistic regression model was used, including potential risk factors such as age, sex, serum albumin level, presence of ILD, pneumothorax history, and heavy smoking history (30 pack-years or more). The significance level was set at p = 0.05. All statistical analyses were performed using EZR (Saitama Medical Center, Jichi Medical University, Saitama, Japan), a graphical user interface for R (The R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria, version 4.0.4) [7].

## Discussion

In this study, ILD was a common factor among patients who did not achieve resolution with chest tube drainage alone or by subsequent single non-operative treatments. Few studies have examined the factors influencing the clinical course of pneumothorax at each stage of treatment. Therefore, we examined the risk factors for treatment failure both during primary treatment with chest tube drainage and during secondary non-surgical treatment in patients ineligible for surgery. The present study revealed that patients with a history of pneumothorax or ILD were less likely to achieve resolution with chest tube drainage alone (Group A vs. B) [1], possibly because once a pneumothorax occurs, the ruptured area becomes friable, making the alveolopleural fistula difficult to seal, and because of ILD fibrosis of the lung, which hinders lung expansion [8]. Multivariable analysis also suggested that younger patients were less likely to achieve resolution with chest tube drainage alone. However, this finding may be attributed to prophylactic surgical referral in many of these cases, where the chest tube was retained, and the patients were referred for surgery.

Patients with pneumothorax that does not resolve with chest tube drainage alone are often considered for surgery, as it is the definitive treatment [1,9,10]. However, surgical invasiveness is more likely to exacerbate conditions such as ILD and COPD, making it difficult for patients to undergo surgery [11-14]. Therefore, nonsurgical treatments are considered as subsequent treatments. In this study (Group C vs. D), patients with a history of heavy smoking or ILD were less likely to achieve resolution with a single non-surgical medical intervention. This may be explained by smoking-related impairment of cells involved in lung repair and fibrotic changes in ILD that hinder lung expansion [14,15].

In this study, we measured the success rate of non-surgical treatment. At our institution, autologous blood is generally preferred owing to its lower risk of side effects and reduced likelihood of exacerbating ILD compared with OK-432 [16]. The resolution rate per autologous blood patch was 10.2-18.5%, markedly lower than the 78% reported previously [17]. The discrepancy may be explained by the smaller number of patients with ILD in previous studies than in our study. We defined resolution as the absence of recurrence for 24 hours after chest tube removal; however, because previous studies did not clearly define their criteria for resolution, treatment success in those reports may have been determined by the disappearance of the air leak alone. Given the minimal side effects described above, the use of autologous blood adhesion should be actively considered in patients such as those in our study. In contrast, the resolution rate with OK-432 was 52.8-67.9%, which is close to the 63% reported previously [16]. In addition, talc use was low in this study because it was not approved for the treatment of pneumothorax in Japan until recently and because talc is generally not used in patients with an active air leak; it is typically instilled after the leak has resolved to prevent recurrence.

This study had some limitations. First, because this study was not limited to ILD, we did not consider the use of corticosteroids, a history of acute ILD exacerbation, or ILD subtype. Further research investigating these factors is needed. Second, this study lacked external validity because it was a single-center retrospective

Third, results may have differed if a continuous variable was used; however, a threshold of 30 pack-years or more was used for heavy smoking history, according to the Lung Cancer Screening Guideline 2022 of the Japanese Lung Cancer Society. Fourth, imaging findings were not considered; therefore, the results may have differed depending on the degree of emphysema and fibrosis. Fifth, the doses of drugs and autologous blood used in pleurodesis were not standardized, although in principle, 50-100 mL of autologous blood and OK-432 were used. Sixth, this study did not consider the extent of pneumothorax or patients’ performance status.

## Conclusions

The study findings indicate that patients with a history of pneumothorax or ILD were less likely to achieve resolution with chest tube drainage alone, whereas those with a history of heavy smoking or ILD were more likely to require additional medical treatment. These easily obtainable clinical characteristics can support early risk stratification at the time of admission and help clinicians anticipate a prolonged air leak or the need for additional interventions in patients who are not candidates for surgery. Integrating these predictors into standardized care pathways may optimize consultation timing, monitoring intensity, and patient counseling.
